nodes.label: Audra Simpson
nodes.date_label: “On Ethnographic Refusal” 2007 · Mohawk Interruptus 2014 · “The Ruse of Consent” 2017
nodes.description: An anthropologist of Kahnawà:ke Mohawk nationhood whose method has become a resource for historians. In 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) she proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' from Iroquois studies, which since Morgan had sought 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them', and she made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in'. History-writing, she argued, 'naturalises this occupation'; her own analysis reaches back through colonial membership law. Indigenous contexts are 'never properly "post-colonial"'. Mohawk Interruptus (2014), as Nicoll's review quotes it, carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's migrations and into Morgan and Parker's ethnology, which became 'a regulatory body of knowledge' used 'to adjudicate claims to land'.

nodes.label: Glen Sean Coulthard
nodes.date_label: Subjects of Empire? (PhD) 2009 · Red Skin, White Masks 2014
nodes.description: A political theorist whose critique of recognition is read by historians of colonial Canada. His 2009 dissertation, the basis of Red Skin, White Masks (2014), set out 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon's critique of Hegel against the liberal recognition that Charles Taylor defended. Reworking Marx's primitive accumulation, he argued that 'the history and experience of dispossession, not proletarianization' had shaped relations with the Canadian state, and that Indigenous anti-colonialism is 'a struggle primarily inspired by and oriented around the question of land'. His alternative, self-recognition, means 'critically revaluating, reconstructing and redeploying Indigenous cultural forms'. He named Taiaiake Alfred, with James Tully, as a mentor.

nodes.label: Emma LaRocque
nodes.date_label: Defeathering the Indian 1975 · dissertation 1999 · When the Other Is Me 2011
nodes.description: A scholar whose criticism of Canadian historical writing began with school textbooks. Her 1974 research for Alberta found 'endless layers of stereotypes … particularly in history and social studies' and led to Defeathering the Indian (1975). Her 1999 dissertation named its targets. James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing was 'eye-opening and ground-breaking' but 'does not go deep enough', for 'Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory showed 'a language of containment'. The 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk framed 'all things Native' as 'cultural differences'. Scholars, 'especially historians and literary critics', must 'comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization'. She drew on Memmi, Fanon and Said, and on Howard Adams's 'White Ideal'. When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.

nodes.label: Chris Andersen
nodes.description: A sociologist whose 'Métis' (2014) challenges the understanding of Métis as 'mixed'. Scholars of 'Métis histories, literatures, and politics' are drawn to 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity'; to the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us', but belonged to colonial projects to 'usurp all the Indigenous territories' on which Canada was built. Peoplehood rests instead on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood'. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall. His 2009 essay asked Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using the disciplines, history among them, that communities themselves use.

nodes.label: Haunani-Kay Trask
nodes.date_label: Review of Linnekin 1986 · “Natives and Anthropologists” 1991 · From a Native Daughter 1993, revised 1999
nodes.description: A scholar of Hawaiian sovereignty whose 1991 reply to Roger Keesing is a founding exchange over who may interpret the Native past. Keesing had argued that Pacific nationalists idealise and 'invent' their pasts. Trask answered with 'solid evidence from Native forms of history-genealogy', charged that Keesing, 'with many Western academics', assumed that 'Natives don't know very much', and insisted 'We do not need, nor do we want to be "liberated" from our past'. She named Lilikalā Kameʻeleihiwa among the Native historians Keesing had not read. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'. Kauanui (2016) credits her essay on 'settlers of color' in Hawaiʻi as an earlier settler-colonial analysis.

nodes.label: Winona Wheeler
nodes.date_label: 'The Othering of Indigenous History' 1998 · 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' 2005 · 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' 2010 · Shekon Neechie 2018 · open letter 2021
nodes.description: Historian of Cree oral tradition and of the academy's treatment of Indigenous history. In 1998 she argued that historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame. Her method writing treats Indigenous oral history 'as source and method in scholarly research': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and the historian 'develops reciprocal relationships with them'. Oral historians, she argues, must learn how knowledge keepers establish their sources ('a traditional footnote'), and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings that guide the learning, keeping, and transmission of Indigenous knowledge' (2010). She learned from Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé, and draws on Ahenakew's published account of Old Men as historians. Leddy (2010) opens her account of community-based history with Wheeler's words on knowledge 'by way of relationships'. She serves on the managing board of Shekon Neechie (2018).

nodes.label: Brenda Macdougall
nodes.date_label: One of the Family 2010 · Clio Prize 2011 · 'Ways of Knowing' symposium 2018 · open letter 2021
nodes.description: Historian of Métis family and community in the northwest. One of the Family (2010) set out 'to contribute … to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'. She read fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell and frames as a Cree worldview of 'relatedness' that 'did not appear in any of the historical records'. Against a historiography 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', she showed Métis people 'actively involved in becoming, rather than passively awaiting identity transmission through external forces and trauma'. In 2018 she co-hosted a symposium on Métis-specific research methods.

nodes.label: Robert Alexander Innes
nodes.date_label: Oral history methods 1999–2000 · insider/outsider 2009 · Elder Brother and the Law of the People 2013 · 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' 2018 · open letter 2021
nodes.description: Historian of Cowessess First Nation, kinship and treaty land, and a critic of how historians have written the 1880s starvation policy. In 2018 he wrote that neither historians nor the Canadian government had acknowledged the starvation deaths of the early 1880s in Treaty 4 territory as genocide, and that historians who agreed the policy killed many had not tried to count the dead. Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research had done that work. Historical records, he argued, do not tell a story by themselves, and decolonizing history can simply mean asking the right questions and looking in the right places. Against Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), he held that Edgar Dewdney bore responsibility and that Daschuk misrepresented Tobias, Lux and Titley, whom he cites. Earlier he wrote on oral history methods in Native Studies and on insider research; he conceived Shekon Neechie (2018).

nodes.label: Mary Jane Logan McCallum
nodes.date_label: 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' 2009 · Indigenous Women, Work, and History 2014 · 'Words for Reading Indigenous Health History' 2017 · 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' 2018 · open letter 2021
nodes.description: Historian of Indigenous labour, health and archives. Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014) follows domestic workers, hairdressers, community health representatives and nurses through state placement programmes, 1940–80; her reviewer Carol Williams notes that she worked with nursing associations who 'granted full access to records', and that her conclusion 'reflects on the professional status and glaring absence of Indigenous historians in academia'. Writing in 2018, she treats archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records were made without Indigenous knowledge or consent, yet remain vital to Indigenous history. She describes interpreting such records together with others rather than alone, and hopes for Indigenous roles in making and keeping records. She sits on the managing board of Shekon Neechie.

Winona Wheeler asks historians to treat Indigenous oral history 'as source and method': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and 'one develops reciprocal relationships with them' (2010). Margaret Kovach locates method in relationship: 'it is not the method, per se' but its congruence 'with an Indigenous worldview' (2010). The Stó:lō field school's teachers wrote that historians 'could no longer in good conscience claim to be writing Aboriginal history when they were not speaking with Aboriginal people'; community staff set the questions and papers return to the Stó:lō archives (2009). Lianne Leddy, researching her own Serpent River First Nation, found university ethics review 'culturally inappropriate' (2010). Mary Jane Logan McCallum treats Indian Affairs archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians (2018). Shekon Neechie (2018) is 'entirely Indigenous conceived, created, and controlled'.

strands.title: Cree oral history as source and method
strands.focus: Wheeler writes as a Cree historian taught by Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé. She treats oral history 'as source and method': knowledge keepers establish their sources within their narratives, 'sort of like a "traditional footnote"', and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings' as well as to study them (2010). Her 1998 critique of 'Indian–White relations' history sits on `native_newcomer`.
strands.works: Cree Intellectual Traditions in History (2010); The Othering of Indigenous History (1998)

strands.title: Relational research methodologies
strands.focus: Indigenous methodologists outside history define method as relationship. Shawn Wilson (Opaskwayak Cree): research is 'the ceremony of maintaining accountability to these relationships' (2008, publisher). Kovach: the conversational method is 'relational at its core'; a decolonizing perspective remains necessary but 'centres the settler discourse' and is 'not the epistemological centre' of an Indigenous methodology (2010). Smith's 1999 agenda is their shared reference. Macdougall (2018) notes that the method texts available to teachers are First Nations-specific.
strands.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999; 2012; 2021); Research Is Ceremony (2008); Indigenous Methodologies (2009); Conversational Method (2010)

strands.title: Kinship, community and the archive
strands.focus: Historians who read documentary records through their communities' concepts and relationships. Macdougall reconstructed community history from HBC, mission and scrip records and read them through wahkootowin, a Cree worldview of relatedness in her framing and a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell, against a historiography 'preoccupied with race at the expense of culture' (2010). Innes points to Cowessess First Nation's own treaty-land research as the count of the 1880s starvation deaths that historians had not made (2018). McCallum describes reading Indian Affairs records about her own community and interpreting them with others (2018).
strands.works: One of the Family (2010); Elder Brother and the Law of the People (2013); 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018); 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018)

strands.title: Research ethics and Indigenous governance of research
strands.focus: TCPS 2's chapter 9 (2010) opens by acknowledging that research 'has been defined and carried out primarily by non-Indigenous researchers'. It requires community engagement, including for 'interpretation of research results that will refer to Indigenous … history', exempts historical research on public records while asking for 'culturally informed advice', and cites OCAP from the First Nations Regional Longitudinal Health Survey (2022 text). SSHRC's 2015 guidelines make 'co-creation of knowledge' essential. The TRC (2015) asked SSHRC, archives and commemoration bodies to act (Calls 65, 70, 77–79). Leddy's 2010 critique shows how review looked from inside a community.
strands.works: TCPS 2, ch. 9 (2010); SSHRC guidelines (2015); TRC Calls to Action (2015); Leddy (2010)

strands.title: Indigenous historians' own institutions
strands.focus: Shekon Neechie (21 June 2018) describes itself as 'entirely Indigenous conceived, created, and controlled'; it counts community-trained and self-taught historians as historians and gives peer feedback from Indigenous historians. Its board (Macdougall, McCallum, Anderson, Corbiere, Hill, Wheeler, Innes) published an open letter supporting the CHA Council's 2021 genocide statement (13 August 2021).

nodes.label: Life Lived Like a Story (Sidney, Smith, Ned and Cruikshank, 1990)
nodes.date_label: Family request 1974 · UBC Press and Nebraska 1990 · paperback 1992 · reviewed 1992 · cited as a model 2009–10
nodes.description: A book credited to Julie Cruikshank 'in collaboration with' three Yukon elders, Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned, who told their life stories; Cruikshank recorded and arranged them. The project began in 1974, when 'younger members of their respective families … asked Cruikshank to record their autobiographies' (McClellan 1992). The narrators chose the form: Sidney and Smith wove personal incidents with 'well-known stories from the traditional narrative repertoire', and Ned 'chose to emphasize songs and oratory'. Cruikshank, Gmelch wrote, 'gradually shifted her research focus from documenting their lives … to examining the actual way they talked about, remembered, and interpreted their lives'. Reviewers called it 'a work of true collaboration between native and non-native' and 'a valuable model of how collaboration between an anthropologist or oral historian and their native teachers can work'; McClellan also noted that Cruikshank 'selected the material' and 'arranged it'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, Annie Ned and Julie Cruikshank, Life Lived Like a Story: Life Stories of Three Yukon Native Elders (Vancouver: UBC Press; Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1990; Bison paperback 1992). edges.relationship: Makes refusal a method: sovereignty 'matters at the level of method and representation', and ethnography becomes a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007, read in full), p. 72 for both quotations; p. 78: refusals 'tell us when to stop' and 'critique and move us away from statist forms of recognition'; p. 75: a foreign culture 'naturalises this occupation through history-writing and the very analytics that are used to know them'. Her own analysis reaches back through colonial membership law (pp. 72–76); interview passages are not used. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Criticises Iroquois studies since Morgan as 'a documentary form' seeking 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them', producing 'anthropologies of timeless, procedural "tradition"' at odds with Six Nations sovereignty (2007)

Nicoll's review essay (2015, read in full) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 93: the Morgan–Parker tradition became 'a regulatory body of knowledge' in a state 'that uses anthropological and historical archives to determine legal presence, to adjudicate claims to land'; the book is known through that reader only. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Reads Kahnawà:ke membership disputes as carrying 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism', with status designations inscribed on persons (2007); refusal as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society' (2017)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74; 2017 abstract (existing source, read). Nicoll (2015) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 3 on 'the structure of settlement that strangles their political form'. edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction pp. 5–6, 13 and 20 (publisher sample, read). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: The racialization of the Métis as mixed was 'part of a larger set of colonial projects through which administrators have attempted to usurp all the Indigenous territories upon which colonial nation-states such as Canada have been produced' (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, introduction pp. 10–11 (publisher sample, read). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Answers Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts with genealogy as 'Native forms of history', against an academic assumption that 'Natives don't know very much'; Keesing and Linnekin replied in the same issue (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991, read in full), pp. 159–161, 164 and 166 n. 4. Replies read: Keesing, the 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy 'a great leap backward' and 'Does she really have to suspend her critical judgment with regard to the past?' (pp. 168–169); Linnekin, 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious' and Trask's view of tradition 'strikingly similar to my own' (pp. 173–174). Neither Keesing nor Linnekin has a node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Kauanui lists Trask's essay on 'settlers of color' in Hawaiʻi (written 1992; published in Amerasia, 2000) among analyses of settler colonialism that preceded Wolfe's (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Named reader: Kauanui 2016, note 7 (reread 2026-10-27; the earlier project reading was in full). Trask's essay itself is unread. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Against the 'invention' thesis, Native nationalists do not need 'to be "liberated" from our past', and Native sources of history must be read (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Own words, 1991, pp. 160 and 164. A passage of Hawaiian knowledge that Trask quotes from Kameʻeleihiwa is not reproduced (OCAP limits). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

edges.relationship: Indigenous oral history 'as source and method': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', relations are reciprocal, and historians must 'apply the teachings'.
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 47 ('Elders are not just repositories of knowledge. They are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers'), p. 48 ('The overarching goal of this paper is to contribute to the growing studies on the value of Indigenous oral history as source and method in scholarly research'; 'one develops reciprocal relationships with them'), p. 59 ('our task is not only to create a space for other ways of knowing as an object or subject of study, but also to create a space to apply the teachings').
edges.map_label: Oral history as source and method

edges.relationship: Wheeler takes Ahenakew's account of the Old Man as historian and 'authentic repository for the annals of his people', and learned from his protégé Stan Cuthand.
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 49 (Cuthand 'followed the path of his mentor Edward Ahenakew'; she met Cuthand in 1982 at Manitoba), p. 53 (Ahenakew, The Plains Cree, on the Old Man as 'an institution in Indian life through the centuries') and p. 56 ('an authentic repository for the annals of his people').

edges.relationship: Historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame and set Indigenous oral history aside (1998).
edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler] 1998, pp. 24–27, read in full (existing nnreq_stevenson_1998, on the native_newcomer roster). Person-level edge beside edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer), which stays. Ends in Agent A's field; A to confirm.

edges.relationship: Knowledge keepers establish source and transmission within their narratives, 'sort of like a "traditional footnote"': oral history needs its own source criticism, learned from the keepers themselves.
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 58: 'Cree historians trained in the oral tradition do not assume omniscient authority'; side stories 'serve to establish the original source(s)' — 'It's sort of like a "traditional footnote."' The narratives and protocols she discusses are not reproduced (OCAP review #1).

edges.relationship: Cree intellectual traditions written 'in history, as history'; co-founder of the Indigenous-controlled Shekon Neechie.
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 48 ('as we carve a space for Indigenous oral history in history, as history'); USask News 2018 on the managing board. Ends in Agent B's field; B to confirm.

edges.relationship: Reads fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept absent from the records that she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell, so that documents can reflect 'the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'.
edges.evidence_note: One of the Family, pp. xi–xii ('My intent … was to contribute in some fashion to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'; the term 'did not appear in any of the historical records', and she credits it to Métis Elder Maria Campbell), p. 3 (her definition, briefly: relatedness with all beings), p. 11 (genealogical reconstruction as method; no genealogies reproduced). Her 2018 Shekon Neechie report (cited, not quoted) treats acknowledging the sources of ideas and stories as a research protocol.

edges.relationship: Canadian Métis historiography was 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', classifying the Métis as 'more white or Indian, more French or British'; Giraud's analysis 'verged on the eugenic'.
edges.evidence_note: One of the Family, p. 14: 'Canadian scholarship tends to focus on how best to classify the Metis – were they more white or Indian, more French or British? In short, Canadian scholars, like their American colleagues, have been overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture'; p. 13 on Giraud; p. 2 on 'Red River myopia'. Fairness: Van Kirk and Brown's work is 'pioneering' (p. 13) and Spry is credited (p. 14). Ends in Agent A's field (parallel to A's Andersen critique of fur_trade_families_metis); A to confirm.

edges.relationship: Daschuk's Clearing the Plains exonerates Edgar Dewdney by misrepresenting the historians it cites, and its praise suggests few readers checked the foundational literature (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced). 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (2018), para. 2 (his aim: to hold Daschuk's argument against the scholars he cites); paras. 5–8 (Tobias 1983, Lux 2004 and Titley 1999 set against Daschuk on Dewdney); para. 14 (whether those who praised the book read the foundational literature). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan', para. 15 (Daschuk's attempt to exonerate Dewdney contradicts previous historians). Daschuk's words are known only through Innes. Ends in Agent B's field (strand health_starvation); B to confirm.

edges.relationship: Historians of the 1880s starvation policy agreed it killed many yet none called it genocide or tried to count the dead; records do not tell a story by themselves (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018), para. 2 (neither historians nor the government acknowledged genocide in Treaty 4 territory; why none counted the deaths); para. 13 (Tobias, Lux, Daschuk and Titley avoid the term); para. 16 (against Woolford's defence of Daschuk: records do not speak for themselves); para. 17 (why historians did not look for the evidence). Fairness: he builds on Tobias and Lux ('Clearing the Plains of Accountability', paras. 5–6). Ends in Agent A's field; A to confirm.

edges.relationship: Points to Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research as the count of the starvation policy's dead that historians never made: history asking the right questions and looking in the right places (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced; the community's figures are not reproduced, OCAP limits). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018), paras. 21–25 (the band's treaty-land researchers traced members missing from annuity lists, work historians had not done); para. 29 (decolonizing history as asking the right questions and looking in the right places). USask News 2018: Innes conceived Shekon Neechie.

edges.relationship: Archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records made without consent are read critically and interpreted together with others (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced; its family material is not used). 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018): opening (archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians); section on Library and Archives Canada (records made under the Indian Act without Indigenous knowledge or consent; still vital to Indigenous history); closing paragraph (an interpretive method that involved other people; restricted records under a researcher agreement). Williams 2016 (BC Studies 191, read in full) on her collaboration with Indigenous nursing associations.

edges.relationship: An Indigenous historian's account of the colonial archive: the state at the door, records made without consent, reading them as their makers did, and the case for Indigenous control of records (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced). 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018), section on Library and Archives Canada: security and registration at the national archives; reading Indian Affairs files requires adopting the department's logic; a hope for Indigenous roles in the making, storage and regulation of records, community-based and at LAC. She cites Susan Hill on the Indigenous research trip to the national archives.

edges.relationship: DuVal: in the Arkansas Valley Native peoples dominated and incorporated colonists; 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Kathleen DuVal's argument (The Native Ground, 2006), not a verdict of the field. Introduction unread; the central sentence, p. 5, is witnessed identically by two readers read here: Piker (AHR 112:3, 2007, extract read) and Isaac (ActiveHistory, 2021, read in full). Piker also quotes p. 5: colonialism 'met neither accommodation nor resistance but incorporation'. Hatfield (Common-Place 7:2, 2007, read in full): DuVal 'argues that unlike the peoples of the Great Lakes region Richard White studies … Arkansas Indians dominated their region well into the nineteenth century … because they were not a population of refugees as were the Indians in the Great Lakes'. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.4)
edges.map_label: DuVal: native ground, not middle ground, 2006

edges.relationship: Hämäläinen: Comanche power left 'little or no middle ground for compromise between Indians and non-Indians' (Grillot on The Comanche Empire, 2008); White's 2011 preface agrees that in this case 'no middle ground emerges'
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Pekka Hämäläinen's book as read by Thomas Grillot (Books & Ideas, 20 January 2014, read in full): 'There is little or no middle ground for compromise between Indians and non-Indians in his book (p. 130): the Comanches are too powerful for this'; Grillot also judges that 'the criticism of the concept of the middle ground … seems here to have been pushed too far'. The book itself is unread. White's own reading of it, 2011 preface p. xv (Google Books snippet, source pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_preface_2011): 'no middle ground emerges'. Grillot records that White signed the preface to the French translation. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.5)
edges.map_label: Hämäläinen: Comanche empire, no middle ground, 2008

edges.relationship: Witgen: in a Native New World the French moved, as Reda puts it, from misunderstanding to being 'essentially delusional' about their relations; European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Michael Witgen's book as read by John Reda (H-AmIndian, July 2014, read in full), p. 2: 'Up to this point, Witgen's explanation seems little different from Richard White's middle ground, where cultural misinterpretations often led to workable understandings between Europeans and Native Americans. Witgen, however, pushes further to demonstrate that the French passed quickly from misunderstanding Native Americans to becoming essentially delusional about the nature of their relationships with them.' Witgen as quoted by Reda: 'the possession of large portions of Native North America by the empires of Europe never occurred' (p. 28); the British 'simply inherited the illusion of empire' (p. 217). 'Delusional' is Reda's word, not Witgen's. The book is unread. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.6)

edges.relationship: White in 2021 (interview published in Portuguese translation): the more anthropology he read, the more critical he became of ethnohistory as a hybrid, and he is increasingly wary of upstreaming; the New Indian History now looks primitive, and its agency argument could go too far
edges.evidence_note: Paraphrase only. Fontella, História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054 (read in full): White's English answers, received 30 April 2021, are published only in Fontella's Portuguese translation, so no English words are attributed to him. p. 10: 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; 'A New Indian History parece bastante primitiva agora … a tendência poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 15: 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16: upstreaming assumes that a belief, ritual or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda significativamente à medida que viaja no tempo'. The later worry about agency is his own; it is not evidence about Brownlie and Kelm's 1994 essay. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

edges.relationship: Proposes 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory from the space of “native North American anthropology”' (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, 'On Ethnographic Refusal', Junctures 9 (2007), read in full by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.1): pp. 70–71 (the quotation); p. 71, Iroquois Studies 'quite literally took off where Morgan left off, and as such is a documentary form' and 'seeks to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them'; Morgan's League 'a paradigmatic text of reconstructed and salvage ethnography'. No individual ethnohistorian is named in those pages, so the arrow goes to the field. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_03); drafted here because the edge ends in ethnohistory. Agent B's ihB_rel_02 (audra_simpson → anthropology) carries the anthropology side.
edges.map_label: Simpson: away from the ethnohistorical paradigm, 2007

edges.relationship: Helped the Newberry Library inaugurate its centre for the study of Indian history (1972) and directed its first fellows (1973–74); Iverson judged that the centre, under Jennings and Hoxie, 'has become an extremely influential place' (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Iverson, introduction to the 1993 reissue of Native American Tribalism, p. v, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.9): 'before his death in 1977, McNickle had helped the Newberry Library of Chicago inaugurate the center for the study of Indian history that now bears his name'; first fellows 1973–74 with McNickle as director; under 'Francis Jennings and Frederick Hoxie, [it] has become an extremely influential place'. Hoxie's remark that it 'has had a clear impact on the writing and teaching of Native American history' is as reported by Iverson and is not used as a quotation here. The 1972 founding and the 1984 naming rest on the existing finding-aid record (indexed). Placed in ethnohistory because the centre's programme belongs to the US Native-centred history that the field's roster (Jennings's successors, Calloway, Richter) represents; Agent B requested it (ihB_rel_26).

edges.relationship: Métis peoplehood, not 'mixedness': the 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity' in scholarship on Métis histories misrecognize the Métis as 'a hybrid off-shoot of two races' rather than an Indigenous people (2014)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), introduction read in the publisher's sample (pp. 3–14): p. 4, 'an overly racialized narrative that connected Métis nationhood to fur trade society'; p. 5, 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories'; p. 6, 'misrecognized as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'; p. 10, 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?'; p. 11, 'To continue to understand the Métis in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions'; p. 12, chapter 1 treats 'a strand of long-standing fur trade literature'. In the pages read he names no fur-trade historian, so the arrow targets the frame, not Van Kirk, Brown or Peterson. Their side in their own words: Peers and Podruchny (2010, n. 2) use 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women'; Brown, as translated there (pp. 2–3, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; Brown (2017, p. 57 n. 26) names The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field and (pp. 57–58) offers 'of mixed descent' as a descriptive term beside 'the natives’ own categories'. Chapters 1–5 unread. Person entry, identity note and the book's source record are Agent B's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§2.1–2.2)

edges.relationship: Judges James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples 'eye-opening' but 'conservative and inadequate': 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (University of Manitoba, 1999), PDF p. 119, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): 'I find James Walker's assessment of Canadian historical writing conservative and inadequate. While Walker's article is an eye-opening and ground-breaking re-assessment of Canadian historiography … it does not go deep enough'; against his conclusion that the times made prejudice inevitable: 'Does any time ever make prejudice … “inevitable”? Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Walker's 1971 survey (nnreq_walker_1971) is in this strand; he has no node. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque at field level; this is the person-level, strand-level arrow. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_16).

edges.relationship: Reads Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory, which praised it for never descending 'to recrimination', as 'a typical example of containment' of Native resistance writing (1999)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (1999), PDF pp. 135–136, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): Native works are 'gauged with a language of containment. Bruce Trigger's foreword to George Sioui's For An American [sic] Autohistory provides a typical example of containment'; scholars 'must make it their mandate first to comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization merely as “sloganistic,” “bitter,” “biased” or “polemical”' (p. 136). Trigger has no node; the arrow goes to the strand that holds his contact-era work. Sioui is not the target. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_17).

edges.relationship: Community-directed and Indigenous-led practice reshapes oral history: relationships, protocols and community review, with interviews and papers returned to the community's own archive.
edges.evidence_note: Rivera describes Aymara direction and return of results (existing rivera_oral reading); 'Each student's field school paper eventually finds its way to the Stó:lō archives, along with digital copies of any conducted interviews' (Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, p. 5); Leddy 2010 pp. 9–15 (storytelling as 'an important way for Indigenous peoples to be active participants and recognized experts in academic research', p. 9); Wheeler 2010 p. 48 ('reciprocal relationships'). Takes over the community-directed parts of edge_125, which stays on `indigenous` for Smith and Wilson.

edges.relationship: Historians of Native–newcomer relations could not 'in good conscience claim to be writing Aboriginal history when they were not speaking with Aboriginal people'; Métis history was 'preoccupied with race at the expense of culture'.
edges.evidence_note: Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, p. 4 (verbatim). Macdougall 2010, p. 14: 'Canadian scholars, like their American colleagues, have been overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture.' Fairness: Macdougall calls Van Kirk and Brown's work 'pioneering' (p. 13), and the Stó:lō authors keep the name ethnohistory. Ends in Agent A's field; A to confirm.
edges.map_label: Speak with the people written about

edges.relationship: Indigenous-led method and Indigenous-authored critique share authors and aims but differ: one is defined by how research is done with communities, the other by Indigenous historical authority and critique.
edges.evidence_note: Wheeler's 1998 critique (nnreq_stevenson_1998) and 2010 method chapter (pp. 47–59); Kovach 2010, p. 42 distinguishes a 'decolonizing perspective' from 'an Indigenous paradigm'; Shekon Neechie 2018 ('entirely Indigenous conceived, created, and controlled'). An editorial comparison between the two parts of the split, agreed with Agent B.

edges.relationship: Community archives and commemoration: field-school papers return to the Stó:lō archives, McCallum hopes for Indigenous roles in making and keeping records, and the TRC asked archives and commemoration to change.
edges.evidence_note: Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, p. 5; McCallum 2018 (section on Library and Archives Canada, paraphrased: a hope for Indigenous roles in the making, storage and regulation of records); TRC Calls 70, 77, 78 and 79(ii) (Call 70 reassembled from a two-column PDF).

edges.relationship: Her agenda of self-determination in research is the shared reference of later Indigenous methodologists and historians; Kovach adds that a decolonizing lens 'is not the epistemological centre' of an Indigenous methodology.
edges.evidence_note: Smith 1999, introduction pp. 1–5 (existing reading). Leddy 2010, p. 2 n. 6 quotes Smith p. 140 on 'indigenous criteria which can judge research "not useful", "not indigenous"' and n. 32 quotes p. 191 on 'the cultural ground rules of respect'; Kovach 2010, p. 42 cites Smith and qualifies the decolonizing lens; Macdougall 2018 lists Smith 1999 among the First Nations-specific method texts.

edges.relationship: Grandmother-to-granddaughter oral history 'rooted in a deep sense of kinship responsibility' and the authority of tribal and family historians become a model for historians researching their own communities.
edges.evidence_note: Wilson 1996 (AIQ 20:1, pp. 3–5) read in full (existing wilson_indian_history). Leddy 2010, p. 10 quotes Wilson's 'Grandmother to Granddaughter' (AIQ 20:1, pp. 7–13; unread) for its method phrase 'a deep sense of kinship responsibility'; the personal passage is not reproduced (OCAP review #8).

edges.relationship: Three Yukon elders and an anthropologist made life histories at the families' request in forms the narrators chose; reviewers called it 'a work of true collaboration', and historians later cite the four as their precedent.
edges.evidence_note: McClellan 1992 pp. 205–206 (1974 family request; narrators' forms; 'a work of true collaboration between native and non-native'); Gmelch 1992 p. 86 ('a valuable model of how collaboration … can work'); cited with all four names by Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009 (p. 2 n. 4) and Leddy 2010 (p. 2 n. 5). Cruikshank's selection and ordering (McClellan p. 205) is kept. Book unread.

edges.relationship: Shifts the oral historian's question from documenting lives to 'the actual way they talked about, remembered, and interpreted their lives', and shows the limits of the Western life-history form.
edges.evidence_note: Gmelch 1992 pp. 85–86 (her own words: the shift of focus; 'a cautionary reminder of the limitations of the conventional life history or autobiographical form'). McClellan quotes Cruikshank that 'autobiography is a culturally specific narrative genre' (p. x) and oral tradition is 'a window on the ways in which the past is culturally constituted and discussed' (p. 14), as quoted by McClellan p. 205. Replaces the Yukon part of edge_125.

edges.relationship: Reviewed as 'a sophisticated and ground-breaking contribution to anthropological scholarship and practice' that points to a new relationship between Native peoples and anthropologists.
edges.evidence_note: McClellan 1992 p. 206: 'Embodying mutual respect and understanding, this book points to the kind of relationship between native Americans and anthropologists that both groups can increasingly hope for'. edge_042 (anthropology → indigenous) stays for Buck, Smith and Wilson.

text_revisions.new: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. In the Great Lakes, White's The Middle Ground (1991) found accommodation in the long periods when 'whites could neither dictate to Indians nor ignore them'. From 2006 critics set his case inside a wider field of Native power: for DuVal 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006); Hämäläinen's Comanches left little room for one (2008); Witgen held that European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012). text_revisions.old: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
text_revisions.new: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, treaties, schools, missions, health and labour. Later work studied reserves (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), treaties (Ray, Miller and Tough 2000), health (Kelm 1998), labour (Lutz), voyageurs (Podruchny 2006), authenticity (Raibmon 2005) and Stó:lō historical consciousness (Carlson 2010). Critics questioned the frame: Brownlie and Kelm on agency as alibi (1994), Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) on its reliance on one side's records, Andersen on reading Métis through 'mixedness' rather than peoplehood (2014). In 2010 Peers and Podruchny wrote that the field had moved 'far beyond older narratives'; in 2021 the CHA Council said historians had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to face this history.

text_revisions.new: Historical writing, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors, from early manuscript and print witnesses to academic history and political theory. It is plural: Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Dakota, Māori, Hawaiian and Aboriginal traditions have their own roots and are not branches of one academic field. From 1969 Deloria, Adams, LaRocque, Sioui, Trask and Smith turned criticism on the institutions and disciplines that studied them; LaRocque judged that 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999). After 2000 the criticism became theory: Audra Simpson's 'ethnographic refusal' (2007, 2014); Coulthard's case against 'the politics of recognition' (2009, 2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's resurgence, which turns from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (2014); Andersen's Métis 'peoplehood' against 'mixedness' (2014). Older university scholarship about Indigenous peoples and community-engaged research have their own entries; settler colonial studies is a comparative field.

field_sets.expect: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.
field_sets.value: Part 1 of the Indigenous histories family (revision 1.201): mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian scholarship about Indigenous–newcomer relations, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology, anthropology and, increasingly, oral history. Francophone work is thin (Delâge, Sioui) and was not surveyed after 2000. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. strand.title: Parks, game laws and dispossession
strand.focus: Settler historians of conservation: Binnema and Niemi (2006) on the Stoney excluded from Banff for game, sport, tourism and assimilation; Sandlos (2007) on northern game laws and sanctuaries as the state's authority over Dene and Inuit hunting; Spence (1999) on Indian removal and the national parks as the United States comparison. Carried over from Indigenous history's 'Land' strand in revision 1.201; O'Brien's Natick history stays there. The environment entry carries the same scholarship in its own strand.
strand.works: Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007)

strand.title: Treaty histories
strand.focus: Ray, Miller and Tough's history of the Saskatchewan treaties draws 'on a wide range of documentary sources' to show how the treaties were shaped by Hudson's Bay Company diplomacy, eastern treaty practice and western change, and why misunderstandings and disputes followed (2000, publisher's description). Miller's general history of treaty-making followed (2009).
strand.works: Ray, Miller and Tough, Bounty and Benevolence (2000); Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009)

strand.title: The field's accounts of itself after 2000
strand.focus: In 2010 Peers and Podruchny called Aboriginal history 'one of the most significant changes in Canadian historiography since the 1970s', said it had 'moved far beyond older narratives', and criticised archive-only work for 'shallow ethnocentric interpretations'; Brown's collected essays (2017) revisit her own terms. In 2021 the Canadian Historical Association's Council stated that historians 'have often been reticent to acknowledge this history as genocide' and had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to come to grips with it. In 2022 Fraser and Stevenson evaluated 'the foundations of professional historical writing in Canada' in the light of the TRC (abstract).
strand.works: Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places (2010); Brown, An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017); CHA Council statement (2021); Fraser and Stevenson, CHR (2022)

strand.title: Historical consciousness in ethnohistorical history
strand.focus: Carlson's study of Stó:lō identity combines, in Knickerbocker's words, 'a long historical view with a micro-ethnohistorical lens' and 'extensive use of oral history interviews' with Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal archives (2010). It rests on two decades of work with the Stó:lō; the community–university practice itself belongs to Community-engaged research.
strand.works: Carlson, The Power of Place, the Problem of Time (2010)

strand.title: Refusal, resurgence and the critique of recognition
strand.focus: Three linked but distinct arguments, each with its own target. Audra Simpson proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014) carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's history and Morgan and Parker's ethnology. Coulthard challenged 'the now commonplace assumption' that colonial relations in Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon against Taylor and reworking Marx: 'dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped Indigenous–state relations (2009; book 2014). Leanne Betasamosake Simpson defined resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and met the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal' (2014), citing Coulthard on recognition and Simpson on refusal. Alfred's Wasáse (2005) is a shared reference. In the pages read none of them criticises Wolfe.
strand.works: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007), Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Glen Sean Coulthard, Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009), Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017)

strand.title: Peoplehood against mixedness
strand.focus: Andersen argues that Métis are misrecognised 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'. To the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us'. Peoplehood rests on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (2014). His 2009 essay asks Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using disciplines including history. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall.
strand.works: Chris Andersen, 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)
